name: KE diet

card.summary: A short, clinic-run programme (also called the KEN or feeding-tube diet) in which a nasogastric tube delivers a liquid formula so the person loses fat quickly and looks leaner.
card.aka: Ketogenic enteral nutrition, KEN diet, feeding tube diet
card.note: Involves a nasogastric tube and very low energy intake; dietitians have questioned its safety and muscle loss.

quick.overview:
The KE diet, usually called ketogenic enteral nutrition (KEN) or the feeding-tube diet, is a rapid weight-loss programme. A thin tube runs through the nose into the stomach and a pump delivers a liquid formula continuously for about ten days. People use it to slim down faster than ordinary dieting allows, for a visibly leaner face and body.

It was devised by an Italian surgeon, Gianfranco Cappello, and its main published data come from its developers and clinic records, which report fat making up a majority of the weight lost. Independent dietitians say the claimed figures lack published support and raise concerns about muscle loss and regain.
quick.how: The programme is delivered through a clinic, which fits the tube, supplies the pump and formula, and monitors the patient. Courses run roughly ten days, with a rest period between repeat cycles. Marketing material from UK clinics cites losses of several percent of body weight per cycle.
quick.risks: Reviewers list tube dislodgement, formula entering the lungs, infection, constipation, muscle loss and weight regain. Commentators say feeding tubes are normally used in hospitals for people unable to eat, and that wearing a tube carries a social burden. Cycles are expensive.

lead: The KE diet, more commonly called ketogenic enteral nutrition (KEN) or the feeding-tube diet, is a commercial weight-loss method in which a narrow tube is passed through the nose into the stomach and a liquid formula is delivered continuously by a pump, day and night, for about ten days [1]. People seek it as a quick way to lose body fat for a slimmer, leaner appearance.

The approach is credited to Gianfranco Cappello, a surgeon at La Sapienza University hospital in Rome, and was introduced to the UK market by gastroenterologist Ray Shidrawi, according to a review by an Irish dietitian [1]. Estimated intake during a cycle is very low, described in that review as around 130 kcal per day, and repeat cycles require a rest period [1].

Proponents of the method report in clinic-based analyses that most of the weight lost is fat, whereas the Irish dietitian's review says the marketed loss figures have no published studies on muscle loss behind them [1].

chain: Tube-delivered low-calorie formula for about 10 days
angle.text: The programme aims at fast fat loss over a short supervised period, which changes facial and body leanness. Providers market per-cycle percentages of body weight lost.

infobox: About 10 days per cycle, with rest between cycles
About EUR 470 (GBP 375) per cycle plus pump deposit

paras: A clinician inserts a narrow nasogastric tube and a pump runs a liquid protein formula continuously for ten days; cycles require a ten-day rest between them [1].

Marketing cites 4 to 9 percent of initial body weight lost per ten-day cycle, a figure the reviewing dietitian says is not backed by published studies on muscle loss [1]. The review reports a price of about EUR 470 (GBP 375) per cycle plus a pump deposit, and estimates several thousand euros to lose 30 kg over 5 to 8 cycles at the claimed rate [1].

The dietitian's review lists tube dislodgement, food entering the lungs, infection if the tube is not cared for, probable muscle wasting, and weight regain, and says feeding tubes should be used only under hospital supervision for people unable to eat [1]. It also raises the social impact of wearing a tube [1].

No independent randomised trial of the feeding-tube method is cited in the review [1]. Separately, mouse studies of ketone ester diets (a different meaning of the abbreviation KE) report lower body weight and adiposity in animals; they are not studies of the feeding-tube method [2].

refs.title: Exogenous Dietary Ketone Ester Decreases Body Weight and Adiposity in Mice Housed at Thermoneutrality
